# Prescriptive lessons -- jamey-aebersold x vol-1-how-to-play-jazz-and-improvise

## maj7
Aebersold treats the major 7th chord primarily through avoidance of the 4th as a phrase-endpoint and elevation of the 6, maj7, 9, and #4 as the signature color tones. The bebop major scale (with added #5 passing tone) and the Lydian mode (major with raised 4th) are the two structural scale options beyond basic major. The #4/raised-4th appears on both the color-tone list and as the defining feature of Lydian, making it the single most-emphasized expressive degree for major harmony.

- [ch.2 p.6] The 4th scale degree carries strong tension on major chords and must not anchor phrase endings; treat it as a passing tone between the 3rd and 5th.
- [ch.7 p.25] The preferred color tones for major chords are the 6, major 7th, 9, and #4 -- the "pretty notes" that shape the tension-release arc within a phrase.
- [ch.8 p.28] The major bebop scale inserts a chromatic passing tone (#5 / G# on C major) between the 5th and 6th degrees, producing an 8-note pattern that aligns chord tones to strong beats.
- [ch.10 p.32] The Lydian scale (C D E F# G A B C) is described as "a beautiful sound and much used" -- a first-cousin to the major scale distinguished by its raised 4th.

## min7
Dorian is the non-negotiable default; pure natural minor (Aeolian) is explicitly ranked last and rarely used. Beyond Dorian, the preferred ordering is Bebop -> Melodic -> Blues -> Pentatonic -> remaining options, giving the improviser a clear hierarchy rather than an open palette. The blues scale may substitute for Dorian only on static minor chords of two or more measures, and must be alternated with Dorian -- not used exclusively -- to preserve variety.

- [ch.2 p.7] The Dorian mode is the mandated minor scale throughout the volume; it relates to the major scale whose root sits a whole step below the Dorian root (e.g., F Dorian = Eb major fingering).
- [ch.7 p.25] The characteristic color (tension) tones for minor chords are the 4, 6, major 7th, and 9th -- to be deployed consciously within the tension-release arc.
- [ch.8 p.28] The dominant 7th bebop scale and the minor ii chord share sufficient common tones to substitute for each other in a ii-V context, allowing one scale to cover both chords.
- [ch.10 p.32] The minor pentatonic built on the chord root is the direct first-choice pentatonic option for minor 7th chords.
- [ch.11 p.38] Target the 3rd and 7th of the min7 chord as primary melodic destinations to internalize the chord's sound before expanding vocabulary.
- [ch.12 p.41] The blues scale may be used over minor 7th chords sustained for 2 or more measures; alternate it with Dorian (same root) to maintain variety.
- [ch.12 p.41] For extended minor sections, alternating Dorian and the blues scale on the same root is the recommended variety strategy.
- [ch.15 p.53] Pure natural minor (Aeolian) is explicitly ranked last in preference among all minor scale choices and is rarely deployed.

## dom7
Aebersold builds a seven-scale palette for dominant 7th, organized by tension level from basic Mixolydian through Bebop, Lydian Dominant, Whole-Tone, Diminished, Diminished Whole-Tone, and Spanish/Jewish. The bebop dominant scale is mechanically privileged: its added chromatic tone (B natural on C7) must always fall on an upbeat, and it doubles as a substitute for the minor ii chord. The 4th degree is the chief danger zone -- permissible only as a passing tone, never as a phrase-ending note.

- [ch.2 p.6] The 4th scale degree on dominant 7th chords carries strong tension and must not end a phrase; treat it strictly as a passing tone between the 3rd and 5th.
- [ch.16 p.54] The 4th-as-passing-tone rule is repeated: "Be careful how you treat the 4th tone. Use it as a passing tone."
- [ch.7 p.25] The "pretty notes" for dominant 7th chords are the 6, major 7th, 9, and #4 -- the same color-tone list shared with maj7.
- [ch.8 p.28] Strong beats (1 and 3) should carry roots, 3rds, 5ths, 7ths, and 9ths; b9s are specifically appropriate on beats 1/3 when the dom7 resolves up a perfect 4th.
- [ch.8 p.28] The dominant bebop scale adds B natural (major 7th) as a chromatic passing tone to C Mixolydian: C D E F G A Bb **B** C. This 8-note pattern aligns chord tones to downbeats.
- [ch.8 p.28 / ch.16 p.54] The added bebop tone (B natural) must always fall on an upbeat -- never on a downbeat. Violating this destroys the jazz-idiomatic alignment.
- [ch.8 p.28] The dominant bebop scale can substitute for the minor ii chord in a ii-V progression; the two chords are interchangeable over the scale.
- [ch.11 p.38 / ch.19 p.65] Emphasize the 3rd and 7th as primary melodic targets on dom7 chords; they are the structurally defining tones.
- [ch.11 p.39] Approach the 3rd or 7th of a dominant chord by half step to strengthen harmonic clarity and produce idiomatic bebop voice-leading.
- [ch.16 p.54] Dominant 7th chords gravitate toward resolution up a perfect 4th (C7 -> F); altered tones resolve by half step to scale or chord tones of the target chord.
- [ch.16 p.54] Seven scale options are available over dom7, in ascending tension: Mixolydian, Bebop, Lydian Dominant (C7#4), Whole-Tone (C7+), Diminished (C7b9), Diminished Whole-Tone (C7+9), Spanish/Jewish. Experimenting across all of them is explicitly prescribed.
- [ch.16 p.54 / ch.7 p.25] The Lydian Dominant scale (Mixolydian + #4) is singled out as a "favorite" color option; its #4 also appears on the pretty-notes list.
- [ch.16 p.54 / ch.18 p.61] The Whole-Tone scale (6 tones, symmetrical) applies to augmented dominant chords (C7+); only two whole-tone scales exist, covering all 12 roots in pairs.
- [ch.16 p.54] The Spanish/Jewish scale (C Db E F G Ab Bb C = F harmonic minor) is the idiomatic choice when a dominant 7th appears in a minor-key context.

## min7b5
Half-diminished chords occupy a distinctive position: they are the one context where the 4th degree may be freely emphasized rather than avoided, reversing the rule that governs major and dominant harmony. A dedicated bebop scale exists for this quality. The chord arises diatonically as a native chord of the minor scale (built on the 6th degree of Dorian).

- [ch.2 p.6] Unlike major and dominant contexts, the 4th degree may be freely emphasized on half-diminished chords -- an explicit reversal of the standard 4th-avoidance rule.
- [ch.8 p.28] The half-diminished bebop scale formula: C Db Eb F Gb **G** Ab Bb C, where G natural is the added chromatic passing tone producing the 8-note pattern.
- [ch.12 p.41] Half-diminished 7th chords are one of the four diatonic seventh-chord types native to the minor scale (alongside maj7, min7, and dom7), arising naturally on the 6th degree of Dorian.

## dom7b9
The dom7b9 symbol is deceptive: it implies one alteration but activates a full 8-note symmetrical diminished scale carrying three altered tones (b9, #9, #4). The b9 is rhythmically appropriate on strong beats specifically when the chord resolves up a perfect 4th.

- [ch.15 p.53 / ch.16 p.54] C7b9 appears to have only one alteration but its underlying diminished scale contains three: b9, +9, and +4. Full scale: C Db D# E F# G A Bb C -- an 8-tone symmetrical structure.
- [ch.8 p.28] The b9 is specifically appropriate on beats 1 and 3 when the dominant chord resolves up a perfect 4th, making it a structurally targeted -- not merely coloristic -- alteration.

## dom7alt
The altered dominant (C7+9) is the maximum-tension dominant option, defined by four simultaneous alterations (b9, #9, #4, #5) via the Diminished Whole-Tone / Super Locrian / Altered Scale. The chord symbol is systematically misleading: C7+9 visually suggests only a raised 9th, but the actual scale content must be internalized in full.

- [ch.15 p.53] The chord symbol C7+9 implies only a raised 9th but the full altered scale contains b9, +4, and +5 as additional alterations. Full scale: C Db D# E F# G# Bb C.
- [ch.15 p.53 / ch.16 p.54] The Diminished Whole-Tone scale (also called Super Locrian or Altered Scale) is the prescribed vehicle for dom7alt; its four altered tones collectively generate maximum harmonic tension.
- [ch.16 p.54] The defining characteristic of this scale is tension production via four simultaneous alterations -- it is positioned at the high-tension end of the dominant scale palette.

## blues-scale
The blues scale is a colorant, not a primary vocabulary -- its six-note formula (root, b3, 4, #4, 5, b7) is fixed, but deployment is deliberately constrained. It must be played as licks and fragments, never as scalar runs; it must be balanced against regular scale usage; and its characteristic harmonic clash with the underlying chord is not an error but the source of its idiomatic sound. Once mastered, additional tones may be incorporated to expand variety.

- [ch.12 p.41] Fixed six-note formula: root, b3, 4, #4, 5, b7 (e.g., F Ab Bb B C Eb F). This formula is universal across all roots.
- [ch.12 p.41] The blues scale sounds wrong when played straight up or down; jazz players deploy bits, pieces, and licks extracted from it -- not scalar runs.
- [ch.12 p.41 / ch.19 p.65] Overuse is explicitly warned against at two points: "Don't run it in the ground" and "may become tiring if you don't also use the regular scales for variety."
- [ch.11 p.39] The clash between blues-scale tones and the underlying harmony is intentional and idiomatic -- it is the source of the blues sound, not an error to correct.
- [ch.12 p.41] The blues scale conveys a specific and bounded expressive character: funky, down-home, earthy, bluesy. It is a tonal character tool, not a general-purpose scale.
- [ch.11 p.39 / ch.12 p.41] The blues scale functions as a horizontal overlay applicable across dominant 7th and minor 7th chords alike; on static minor chords of 2+ measures it is an explicit alternative to Dorian.
- [ch.12 p.41] After the core six-note scale is internalized, additional tones may be incorporated to expand its harmonic variety -- treated as an advanced refinement, not a starting point.
